title: Clear water in March
summary: A short March morning on the Skunk Harbor trail at Lake Tahoe: Christian rode down to the shore and back up with Marley along, and spent most of two hours flying a drone over clear water, snowy granite and the posts of an old dock while Marley went swimming.

post.title: Clear water in March
post.body:
I started rolling just before nine on March 14, headed down the Skunk Harbor trail to Lake Tahoe with Marley along. The bike was just the way down to the water and back up again: about three miles, a little under six hundred feet of climbing, and only twenty-two minutes of actual moving. The whole morning took a bit over two hours.

## The drone's morning

The rest of the time went to the drone. Skunk Harbor is a place where it's allowed, and I'd wanted to see this stretch of shore from above. Mornings with Marley tend to go like that. We get there, and then nobody's in a hurry.

Marley went swimming. She's in the drone video, out in that clear water, with snow still on the shore.

> We get there, and then nobody's in a hurry.

## Straight down

The first shots are from about half past nine. There was still snow in patches under the pines and tucked between the granite, and the sun was low enough that the trees threw long shadows far out over the water. Straight down, the lake is so clear the boulders under the surface show every edge, brown and green against the turquoise, with the shallows fading into deep blue farther out.

Just after ten I took the drone along the shore. The forest runs right down to the rocks, and across the lake the mountains were still white.

## The old dock

The last shot is the one I keep coming back to. A small cove, a few old buildings back in the trees, and a line of posts standing in the shallows. The buildings are only shells now, gutted inside and not fit to live in. The posts are what's left of an old dock from long ago. Nothing on top of them now, just the posts and their shadows on the sand.

## Back up the hill

Then it was back on the bike and up the hill. The top speed for the day was around twenty-six miles an hour, which on a three-mile ride tells you how the way down went.

episode.title: The posts in the shallows
episode.script:
Narrated by A.L.T.A.

Just before nine on a March morning, the east shore of the lake was still holding on to its snow. Christian was on his bike, and Marley was with him.

They were headed down the Skunk Harbor trail. The ride itself was a small thing. Down to the water, and later, back up. About three miles in all. A little under six hundred feet of climbing. Twenty-two minutes of moving, from start to finish.

The morning was a little over two hours. So you can guess where the rest of it went.

***

Christian had brought a drone. And Skunk Harbor is a place where flying one is allowed, which he checked, and which I appreciate. I am a guardian of this water, after all, and I like a visitor who reads the rules.

And Marley? Marley went swimming. She is right there in the drone footage, out in that clear water, with snow still on the shore. A dog in my lake in March. I admire her.

The first pictures come at half past nine. And the water in them, well. I have looked at this lake for a very long time, and I still say it. You could count the stones on the bottom. Brown ones, green ones, every edge sharp, lying in turquoise that slowly gives way to a deep, deep blue.

The snow was still there that morning. Pockets of white under the pines, and tucked in between the granite on the shore. The sun was low, and the trees laid their shadows long across the shallows, like fingers reaching for the middle of the lake.

A little after ten, he sent the drone along the shore. The forest runs right down to the rocks there. And far across the water, the mountains were still white.

***

Then came the picture I like best.

A small cove. A few old buildings, quiet in the trees. They are only shells now, gutted inside. Nobody could live in them anymore. And standing in the shallows, a line of posts, walking out into the water one after another.

They are what is left of an old dock, from long ago. Whatever once tied up there is gone. The boards are gone. The posts stayed, and they cast their little shadows on the sand, every clear morning, whether anyone comes to look or not.

That morning, someone came to look. And he had the good sense to keep the frame simple. Just the posts, the water and the light. Knowing what to leave out of a picture is half of taking it.

***

Christian has a name for mornings like this one. He calls them mornings with Marley. No big summit, no long miles. A dog, a bike, a shore, and time.

Then it was back up the hill. His top speed that day was about twenty-six miles an hour, and on a three-mile ride, I'll leave you to work out which direction that was.

Three miles of riding. Two hours by the water. The lake has never minded that arithmetic. Neither, it seems, has he.

blocks.title: Airspace etiquette
blocks.text:
Before the drone went up, Christian made sure Skunk Harbor is a place where flying one is allowed. It is, and that is where he flew.

Every clip in this story is real aerial footage from that March morning, including the one of Marley out swimming with the drone overhead. Nothing here was animated with AI.
